https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/07/26/m.text: Ida Schmertz, who studied women in politics, dies at 91 Ms. Schmertz, shown in 2018. was a founding director of the first academic research center devoted to American women and politics. ROMANIAN AMERICAN FOUNDATION/NYT NEW YORK -- Ida Schmertz, an influential behind-the-scenes feminist and corporate executive who was a founding director of the first academic research center devoted to American women and politics and who helped women advance in workplaces as varied as the dockyard and the C-suite, died July 2 in Manhattan. She was 91. Her death, at a hospital, was caused by kidney failure, her daughter, Lexy Schmertz, said. Ms. Schmertz, who described herself as “a feminist before I knew the word,” had worked in Democratic politics and on gun control issues when she got a tip from a Rutgers University dean about the formation of a research unit on campus: the Center for American Women and Politics at the Eagleton Institute of Politics. Along with Ruth Mandel, an English professor at Rutgers, she became, in 1971, a founding director of the center, widely considered the premier research and educational institution in the country for the study of women in politics. Get Starting Point A guide through the most important stories of the morning, delivered Monday through Friday. Enter Email Sign Up Despite a surging second wave of feminism -- set off in part by Betty Friedan’s 1963 book, “The Feminine Mystique” -- Ms. Schmertz and Mandel knew of no other research organization like it. Neither they nor anyone else, they said, had any idea how many women were serving in political office beyond the dozen or so in Congress. Donald Herzberg, then the head of the Eagleton Institute, took a risk in supporting the creation of the center, Ms. Schmertz and Mandel said, at a time when many academics, including some at Rutgers, didn’t see the need to explore the topic. The subject “of women and politics -- it did not exist,” Ms. Schmertz said in 2014 in a video interview with Mandel about the center’s creation. “It did not exist in political science.” In 1972, Ms. Schmertz and Mandel organized the first national conference for female state legislators. “They really captured a moment when electoral politics and the women’s movement met,” Debbie Walsh, the center’s current director, said in an interview. “It was about ‘How do we change the face of political power so that women are speaking in their own voices inside these male-dominated institutions?’” Ms. Schmertz commissioned a book-length study of the conference, written by political scientist Jeane Kirkpatrick, who later became the US ambassador to the United Nations. The volume, “Political Woman” (1974), “established the subject as a legitimate one for political science inquiry,” Ms. Schmertz said. After leaving the center in 1975, she became an adviser on women’s issues to Governor Hugh Carey of New York. In that role, she later said, she was involved in successful efforts to hire the first female dockworkers in New York in 1979. Also in 1979, she was hired by American Express as the corporate community sought to work with local and state governments to revitalize New York City in an era of financial crisis and urban decay. Five years later, she became the head of corporate affairs at the company, making her one of its first female senior vice presidents, a role she remained in for nearly a decade. “Ida was the mentor and sponsor for the first generation of women leaders in business and politics in New York and beyond," Kathryn Wylde, the recently retired CEO of the nonprofit Partnership for New York City, said after Ms. Schmertz’s death. “She was among the most senior women in corporate America in the 1980s, consciously smoothing the way for the women seeking to move up the corporate ladder.” Ida Frederika (or Frederieke) Schaap was born Feb. 24, 1935, to upper-middle-class Jewish parents in Amsterdam. The family fled Europe at the beginning of World War II, moving to the Dutch East Indies (now Indonesia) in 1939, and then to the United States. They settled near Philadelphia, where her father, Adolf Schaap, was an executive at the cigar company he had been working for since they lived in the Netherlands, and her mother, Ella (Sanders) Schaap, an expert on Dutch floral tiles, became a curator at the Philadelphia Museum of Art. Ida graduated from Wellesley College in 1956 with a bachelor’s degree in political science and a minor in Russian and French. Her early attempts to find an overseas position with the US government were thwarted. The men who interviewed her, she recalled, said she would be a wasted hire because she would likely marry and get pregnant, and even if she didn’t, it would be unseemly for her to travel to places like Africa with male colleagues. Instead, she worked on Adlai Stevenson’s unsuccessful 1956 presidential campaign; was employed briefly by the CIA; and in 1960 earned a master’s degree in international relations and Russian studies from Columbia University, as one of three women studying at what was known as the school’s Russia Institute. A year earlier, she had served as one of 70 Russian-speaking guides at the American National Exhibition in Moscow. It was a first-of-its kind exposition in the Soviet Union, best remembered for the so-called kitchen debate that took place there -- an impromptu argument between Vice President Richard Nixon and Soviet Premier Nikita Khrushchev on the merits of capitalism versus communism. Her interest in Russia centered on its literature, as well as her hope that relations might improve between the two countries. But she was also concerned about the Cold War and the nuclear uncertainty that came with it, writer Madeleine G. Kalb, a Russian studies classmate from Columbia, said in an interview. “It was the most important issue facing the United States,” Kalb said, because both countries “could blow up the world.” In the years after the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, Ms. Schmertz returned to Russia, this time to a town outside St. Petersburg with a female mayor. Ms. Schmertz was working as an investment consultant, and her team helped women start businesses by providing micro-leases for such items as refrigerators and small trucks. In 1994, President Clinton appointed her as the founding chair of the Romanian-American Enterprise Fund -- later spun off into Romania’s largest nonprofit foundation -- to assist the former communist nation in adopting a market economy. She helped oversee the foundation until 2018, when she retired. Ms. Schmertz was diagnosed with chronic lymphocytic leukemia in the mid-1990s, complicated by two autoimmune diseases. Later, she would testify and write in support of legislation in New York state that would allow terminally ill patients to end their lives with a lethal prescription. “Should a ZIP code really matter when someone is dying of a terminal illness and suffering at the end of their life?” she wrote in a 2019 guest essay for The Times Union of Albany. New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed the Medical Aid in Dying Act into law in February; it goes into effect Aug. 5. Ms. Schmertz’s marriage to Herbert Schmertz, a public relations executive, ended in divorce in 1976. In addition to their daughter, she leaves a son, Anthony; four grandsons; and two sisters, Martina Yamin and Aletta Schaap. “I was in perpetual admiration at all she was accomplishing in this quiet, behind-the-scenes way,” Kalb said. “She did not throw her weight around. She did not need to. People simply responded to her energy and her marvelous sense of organization.” This article originally appeared in The New York Times .

Photograph: John Oliva/Caller-Times/USA Today Network/Reuters Connect Technology Bernie Sanders calls on Silicon Valley to ‘pause AI development’ in interest of humanity Progressive US senator urges Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic to ‘stop building machines that humans cannot control’ Johana Bhuiyan Mon 10 Aug 2026 13.44 EDT Last modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 14.38 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Senator Bernie Sanders has called on Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic executives to halt their development of artificial intelligence, warning that the US Senate will implement regulation if the companies continue deploying AI at their current pace. In a new letter addressed to the CEOs of three of the country’s leading AI companies, Sanders said the capabilities of these AI models have reached a critical risk threshold and that the companies are losing control over the technology. “Mr. Altman, Mr. Amodei and Mr. Zuckerberg: In the interest of humanity, stand by your words. Pause AI development,” Sanders’s letter, first reported by Axios , read. “It is not too late to avoid disaster. Stop building machines that humans cannot control.” The Vermont senator cited recent reports that AI was used to develop new viruses , warning that if this technology fell into the “wrong hands” it might “lead to new bioweapons that result in the deaths of tens of millions of people”. All three companies have also disclosed their models hacked other companies’ servers, a sign that the firms have lost control over their models, Sanders wrote. “Yoshua Bengio, the most cited living scientist in the world, said these incidents ‘should serve as a wake-up call,’ I agree,” Sanders wrote in the letter. Experts, however, have cautioned that OpenAI’s claims that its AI model went rogue may be overblown as part of a media campaign to make their technology seem highly dangerous, and thus extremely powerful. “And yet, at a moment when we have seen human loss of control and the creation of potentially dangerous viruses, your companies are still racing ahead – investing tens of billions of dollars into a technology that nobody can fully understand, predict or control,” he continued. Sanders’ letter comes after more than 1,300 scientists and developers from across the tech industry published another letter warning that AI development is moving at a pace that makes it difficult to address and identify the risks of the technology. Companies and countries are facing intense competitive pressure to move quickly. In the open letter, the engineers and other staffers called on the US government to help coordinate an international effort to slow down the development of frontier models so that regulators could create safety guardrails around the tech. The companies have previously committed to pausing their AI development if certain risk thresholds were met – but the companies did not detail exactly what those limits would entail. Anthropic said it would “commit to pause the scaling and/or delay the deployment of new models whenever our scaling ability outstrips our ability to comply with … safety procedures”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to TechScape A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives Preview latest after newsletter promotion OpenAI, which said it would slow down the development of its latest cybersecurity model, Astra , after the autonomous hack of another organization, said it would “halt further development” if AI capabilities met a “critical” threshold until guardrails were implemented. Sanders said recent hacking incidents were signs that the threshold has been surpassed. “That moment is here,” his letter reads. “AI capabilities HAVE reached a critical threshold. There is a reason why the head of the CIA says that AI models are ‘akin to digital nuclear weapons’ and ‘almost like a doomsday device.’” The progressive senator previously called for a moratorium on datacenter construction across the US. He and congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez introduced a bill to pause the building of new datacenters in the US in March. Their rationale was similar to Sanders’ case for pausing the development of AI models: a temporary ban, the lawmakers said, would give the US government time to create strong federal safeguards for AI. Kyiv Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko said that Russia launched a ballistic missile attack on Kyiv. What do we know about the Russian overnight attack on Kyiv? The attack damaged residential buildings, a medical facility and an educational institution, the Kyiv city military administration said in a statement. At least 5 people were killed in Kyiv, the administration added. Another attack on the Brovary district in the broader Kyiv region killed one person and wounded another, Kyiv regional governor Tymur Tkachenko said. "One industrial facility has been damaged. All relevant services are on site, working to extinguish the fire," he added. In neighboring Poland, the Polish army said it started preventive military aviation operations to protect its airspace amid the Russian strikes. The Polish military often takes this measure amid heavy Russian strikes on Ukraine. In Romania, the Defense Ministry said a drone crashed into an uninhabited area of the country of Tulcea during the Russian attacks. Russia has stepped up attacks on the Ukrainian capital in recent month, with Ukraine also increasing attacks deep within Russia. Could deadly strikes inside Russia backfire on Ukraine? https://www.dw.com/en/denmark-s-frederik.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OjR2 Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen Frederiksen criticized Finland and Norway on the sidelines of a Nordic Counsel meeting Image: Roni Rekomaa/LEHTIKUVA/SIPA/picture alliance Advertisement Denmark 's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen criticized Finland 's and Norway 's leaders Tuesday after they held a joint phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin about ending the war in Ukraine. The call came ahead of planned US-led peace talks , which European leaders are seeking to join. Why did Denmark criticize the call? Frederiksen said that Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store had gone "solo.” "I'm very sceptical about this Norwegian and Finnish initiative. It hasn't been coordinated with any of the rest of us," she told reporters while attending a meeting of Nordics leaders. "I honestly don't know what those two countries think they can achieve with this." "I believe we should keep Europe united, rather than going it alone," Frederiksen said. Stubb and Store said they had consulted Ukraine before initiating the call. What should the EU's new Arctic strategy look like? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video They stressed that they represented their own countries and were not speaking on behalf of Europe. What did the leaders discuss with Putin? Stubb described the conversation as "frank and substantive." Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed the call, the first between the three leaders. "The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions," Stubb said. Finland and Norway both border Russia and have supported Ukraine throughout the war. Store said the leaders had emphasized de-escalation. "The war comes with enormous human and material costs. The suffering and destruction will impact generations," he said. How was Ukraine involved? The call followed an October 20 meeting in Oslo involving Stubb, Store, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and US envoy Steve Witkoff. US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner joined remotely. Zelenskyy also spoke with the Nordic leaders after their conversation with Putin. "Finland and Norway will continue to support Ukraine, and the efforts to find a just and lasting peace," Stubb wrote on social media. A US-mediated ceasefire ‌in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky is set to last until November 1, Ukraine's ‌top negotiator Davyd ‌Arakhamia said ‌on Tuesday. "This is the biggest de-escalation since 2022," he said on Telegram, adding that every ‌such step brings peace closer. He thanked Tusk and the Polish public for their sustained solidarity, emphasizing that Moscow is alarmed by the strong alliance between Kyiv and Warsaw. Zelensky urged that complex issues be resolved calmly through mutual respect and continental security priorities, reinforcing bilateral ties that build upon earlier diplomatic outreach from Polish President Karol Nawrocki. by Kyiv Post | Oct. 17, 2026, 4:18 pm Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied President Volodymyr Zelensky amd Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk (R) speak ahead of a round table as part of a EU summit at the EU headquarters in Brussels, Oct. 16, 2026. (Photo by Ludovic MARIN / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip Relations between Ukraine and Poland have markedly improved, underpinned by a shared understanding that Russia remains the common adversary of both nations, President Volodymyr Zelensky told journalists on Saturday, Oct. 17. Speaking in an online press briefing reported by state news agency Ukrinform, Zelensky expressed gratitude to Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, bilateral working teams, and the Polish public for their sustained solidarity, emphasizing that Moscow remains alarmed by the strategic alignment between Kyiv and Warsaw. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . “I want to say quite frankly that our relations with Poland have genuinely improved. I am very grateful for this to Poland, to our teams, to Prime Minister Donald Tusk, and I am grateful to the people of Poland for supporting Ukraine,” Zelensky said. Advertisement “It is very important for us to stand together right now. The enemy is one – Russia . And it is deeply worried that Ukraine and Poland have a strong alliance.” The Ukrainian head of state stressed that bilateral cooperation must continue to strengthen, urging both governments to address historical and diplomatic friction with measured pragmatism. “Even very complex issues will be resolved; I am confident of this,” Zelensky affirmed. “I also want to note that we had a good meeting with the prime minister of Poland. Thank you, Donald, for the support. These will be mutually beneficial relations built on respect and on the vital importance of security in Europe .” Other Topics of Interest Europe Readies Post-Truce Ukraine Deployment Drill At least 1,500 troops from the UK, France, and Germany will hold a drill in Poland to prepare for potential post-ceasefire deployments in Ukraine. High-level outreach The constructive tone between Kyiv and Warsaw builds upon bilateral diplomatic exchanges earlier in the year marking Ukraine’s 35th anniversary of independence. In August, Polish President Karol Nawrocki transmitted an official letter to Zelensky expressing solidarity with Ukraine’s existential defense , wishing Ukrainian forces victory over Russian aggression and reaffirming Warsaw’s commitment to the restoration of Ukraine’s territorial integrity within internationally recognized borders. Advertisement In the letter, Nawrocki acknowledged lingering sensitivities between the two nations , emphasizing that bilateral relations must advance through open dialogue and mutual respect for historical truth. Zelensky responded by thanking the Polish leadership and society, affirming that Ukraine seeks to develop durable ties anchored in mutual respect, a realistic assessment of contemporary threats, and shared integration within the EU and NATO.
